title: Plan where every content hash survives
description: Change the artifact shape, version history, churn, cache link mode, and remote retention. The estimates show why metadata, local cache, and shared storage are different responsibilities.

datasets.label: Image directory
datasets.detail: Many independently hashed files let unchanged images be reused between versions.

datasets.label: Partitioned Parquet
datasets.detail: Daily partitions bound churn better than rewriting one full historical export.

datasets.label: Model checkpoint
datasets.detail: One rewritten binary usually produces one completely new cached object.

cacheModes.label: Copy
cacheModes.detail: Broadly compatible, but the workspace consumes another full artifact-sized copy.
cacheModes.caveat: Budget both cache bytes and workspace bytes.

cacheModes.label: Reflink
cacheModes.detail: Copy-on-write clones avoid an immediate second copy on supported filesystems.
cacheModes.caveat: Verify filesystem support and measure copy-on-write growth.

cacheModes.label: Hardlink
cacheModes.detail: Low initial overhead, but unsafe in-place writes can mutate the cached inode.
cacheModes.caveat: Treat linked outputs as read-only and validate tool behavior.

remoteStates.label: All referenced objects retained
remoteStates.detail: Every supported Git revision can fetch its exact hashes from shared storage.

remoteStates.label: Only the latest version retained
remoteStates.detail: The newest revision restores, but historical Git pointers can reference deleted objects.

remoteStates.label: Objects never pushed
remoteStates.detail: Only this machine's cache has the bytes; Git metadata has already been shared.

notice: The estimate assumes changed files are the only new content and ignores compression, metadata overhead, multipart behavior, filesystem allocation, and provider pricing. Measure real cache and transfer usage before setting capacity or retention policy.
